questions.q: Why does scarcity force every economic agent to make choices?
choices: Resources used one way cannot be used another
questions.why: Limited resources mean every use rules out another. Rising prices are a symptom, not the cause.

questions.q: What is meant by the term scarcity?
choices: A temporary lack of a good
questions.why: Scarcity is permanent. A shortage is the temporary one.

questions.q: What is the reward to enterprise?
questions.why: Enterprise takes the risk, so it earns what is left over: profit.

questions.q: A student spends £20 on a concert ticket instead of a video game. What is the opportunity cost?
questions.why: Opportunity cost is the next best alternative given up, measured in the alternative rather than in money.

Scarcity.p: The {key|basic economic problem} is that human wants are unlimited but the resources available to satisfy them are limited.

Scarcity.def: the situation where {def|wants are unlimited but the resources to satisfy them are limited}

list: {key|Consumers} have limited income and must choose which goods and services to buy.
{key|Producers} have limited inputs and must choose what to produce.
{key|Governments} have limited tax revenue and must choose which public services to fund.

Scarcity.watch: Scarcity is not a shortage: {exam|a shortage is temporary and happens when demand exceeds supply at the current price, whereas scarcity is permanent}.

Factors of production.p: Resources are also called {key|factors of production}. There are four.

Factors of production.def: {def|all natural resources, such as minerals, forests, fish and the land itself}; the reward to land is {key|rent}
{def|the human effort, both physical and mental, used in production}; the reward to labour is {key|wages}
{def|man-made goods used to produce other goods}, such as machinery, tools, factories and computers; the reward to capital is {key|interest}
{def|the willingness to take risks and organise the other three factors}; the reward to enterprise is {key|profit}

Factors of production.eg: The quality of labour rises with education and training, and the quantity of capital rises with investment.

Opportunity cost.def: {def|the next best alternative forgone when a choice is made}

Opportunity cost.p: It is measured in terms of the alternative given up, {exam|not in money}.

Opportunity cost.eg: If a student spends £20 on a concert ticket instead of a video game, the opportunity cost of the concert is the video game.

Production possibility curves.def: {def|the maximum combinations of two goods an economy can produce when all its resources are fully and efficiently employed}

list: Points on the curve are {key|productively efficient}.
Points inside show unemployed or inefficiently used resources.

Production possibility curves.p: The curve is usually {key|concave to the origin}, because resources are not equally suited to producing both goods.

Economic systems.p: Every economy must answer three questions: {key|what to produce, how to produce it, and for whom}.

list: A {key|market economy} answers them through the price mechanism.
A {key|planned economy} answers them through government decisions.

Specialisation and the division of labou.def: {def|production split into separate tasks, each done by a different worker}

list: Workers become more skilled through repetition
Time saved from not switching tasks

Specialisation and the division of labou.watch: The disadvantages count too: {exam|boredom, a narrow range of skills, and the whole process stopping if one stage fails}.

cards.heading: Unlimited wants and limited resources
cards.body: Human wants are unlimited but the resources available to satisfy them are limited. This situation is called **scarcity** (the condition where resources are insufficient to meet all desires). Because of scarcity, every economic agent must make choices about how to use limited resources.

points.text: a student with £10 must choose between buying a book or a snack.
a farmer with limited land must decide whether to grow wheat or barley.
a council with a fixed budget must choose between repairing roads or building a library.

cards.heading: Scarcity versus shortage
cards.body: Scarcity is a permanent condition due to limited resources relative to unlimited wants. A **shortage** (a temporary excess of demand over supply at a given price) is different. Shortages can be resolved by price changes or increased supply, but scarcity cannot be eliminated.
cards.example: Even if the price of oil rises and supply increases, scarcity remains because wants still exceed available resources.

checks.q: Why does scarcity force every economic agent to make choices?
choices: Resources used one way cannot be used another
checks.why: Limited resources mean every use has an alternative that is given up. Rising prices are a symptom, not the cause.

cards.heading: Four ingredients of everything made
cards.body: Every good and service is made from the same four **factors of production** (the resources used to produce goods and services). Each one earns its own reward.

points.text: every natural resource, from minerals to fish. It earns rent.
human effort, physical and mental. It earns wages.
man-made tools and machines. It earns interest.
